yowie.name: Town and Country Journal on the 'hairy man of the wood'
yowie.summary: In November 1876 the Australian Town and Country Journal printed what is often cited as the earliest newspaper account, passing on Aboriginal reports of an 'unearthly animal' the writer called the Yahoo-Devil Devil, or hairy man of the wood.

yowie.name: McCooey's 'indigenous ape'
yowie.place: Between Batemans Bay and Ulladulla, New South Wales
yowie.summary: Amateur naturalist Henry James McCooey said he saw a tailless, five-foot ape on the south coast, covered in long black hair with reddish fur on its throat and chest. He threw a stone and it ran off. He then offered to catch one for the Australian Museum for a reward of 40 pounds.

yowie.name: A future senator's school-trip sighting
yowie.summary: Bill O'Chee, later a Queensland senator, told the Gold Coast Bulletin he saw a creature over three metres tall on a school trip to Springbrook, which he compared to Chewbacca. Springbrook has more yowie reports than anywhere else in Australia.

yowie.name: Mango farmer metres from a hairy figure
yowie.summary: Katrina Tucker said she came within a few metres of a hairy, human-shaped creature on her mango farm near Darwin. Photos were taken of a large footprint, one of several reports from the Acacia Hills area in the late 1990s.

yowie.name: The Piper film
yowie.summary: Canberra bushwalker Steve Piper filmed what he said was an unknown upright animal in the Brindabella mountains. The short clip is still the best-known yowie footage, and like most such film it is too unclear to settle anything.

skunk-ape.name: A car grabbed on a lonely road
skunk-ape.summary: A driver said a hairy figure rushed out of the brush, grabbed his car and pounded on the running board and door for about half a mile before it let go.

skunk-ape.name: A face at the window
skunk-ape.summary: During a run of reports in central Florida, a rural family said an ape-like creature came around their home several times, once walking up to a window at night to look in.

skunk-ape.name: The Broward County skunk ape flap
skunk-ape.summary: From 1971 to 1975 newspapers in Broward County and Miami covered night-time reports of a 5 to 7 foot ape with dark red to black hair, said to have stalked people and killed a farmer's horse and bull. One officer said he hit it with his car. Posses went out and found nothing, but the coverage made 'skunk ape' a household word in Florida.

skunk-ape.name: A bill to protect 'humanoid animals'
skunk-ape.summary: A bill put to the Florida legislature would have made it illegal to take, possess, harm or molest anthropoids or humanoid animals. It did not pass.

skunk-ape.name: Fire chief photographs a figure crossing the road
skunk-ape.summary: Ochopee fire chief Vince Doerr said he stopped his car and photographed a dark upright figure crossing the road in the swamp. Within two weeks more than fifty people reported a hairy creature in Big Cypress National Preserve, around the time Everglades tour operators said their lima-bean bait stands had been raided.

fouke-monster.name: Memphis Enquirer's hairy wild man
fouke-monster.summary: Long before Fouke, an 1851 report in the Memphis Enquirer told of hunters seeing a large, hairy wild man in Arkansas. It is one of the earliest printed stories people link to the Fouke Monster legend.

fouke-monster.name: A boy fires bird shot at it
fouke-monster.summary: A 14-year-old said he saw a creature with reddish-brown hair sniffing the air. It didn't react when he fired bird shot at it. Early reports like this one came from around Jonesville, and the creature was first called the Jonesville Monster.

fouke-monster.name: Seen crossing Highway 71
fouke-monster.summary: On May 23, 1971, a few weeks after the Ford family attack, D. C. Woods Jr., Wilma Woods and Mrs. R. H. Sedgass said an ape-like creature crossed the highway in front of them. Three-toed tracks turned up in Scott Keith's soybean field soon after, and the game warden couldn't say if they were real.

fouke-monster.name: Fined for a fake monster report
fouke-monster.summary: As hunters poured in, Sheriff Leslie Greer banned guns in the search, and three people were fined 59 dollars each for filing a fraudulent monster report. A Little Rock radio station had put a 1,090 dollar bounty on the creature.

fouke-monster.name: Forty sightings in a year
fouke-monster.summary: Reports had faded by the mid-1970s, but forty sightings were logged in 1997, and in 1998 someone said they saw it in a dry creek bed five miles south of Fouke.

momo.name: Doris Harrison sees it holding a dog
momo.summary: On July 11, 1972, Doris Harrison heard her little brothers screaming in the yard. From the kitchen window she said she saw a huge, dark-haired, man-like creature holding what looked like a dead dog, with a pumpkin-shaped head and glowing orange eyes.

momo.name: The fire chief's headlights
momo.summary: Fire chief and city councilman Richard Murray said a massive upright creature stood in his headlights as he drove along a creek bed. A 20-man posse went out after it and found nothing.

champ.name: Captain Crum's 187-foot serpent
champ.place: Bulwagga Bay, Lake Champlain, New York
champ.summary: The Plattsburgh Republican ran 'Cape Ann Serpent on Lake Champlain', in which a Captain Crum described a serpent about 187 feet long, with three teeth, eyes the colour of peeled onions, a red band round its neck and a white star on its forehead. He said two sturgeon and a billfish followed it.

champ.name: P. T. Barnum offers a reward
champ.summary: The showman P. T. Barnum offered a reward for anyone who could bring him the Lake Champlain monster, and offered again in 1887. Nobody collected.

champ.name: Sheriff Mooney's water serpent
champ.summary: Clinton County Sheriff Nathan H. Mooney said he saw a water serpent 25 to 30 feet long, close enough to make out round white spots inside its mouth. Once a sheriff had spoken up, many more people came forward with their own sightings.

champ.name: The Champlain quote that never was
champ.summary: Vermont Life magazine said Samuel de Champlain saw a 20-foot serpent with a horse's head in 1609. No such line appears in his journals. What he did describe was a big, toothy fish the local people called chaoufarou, which translators later identified as the longnose gar.

champ.name: Clicks recorded under the lake
champ.summary: Working for a Discovery Channel programme, the Fauna Communications Research Institute recorded sounds in the lake like the echolocation clicks of belugas or dolphins, though no animal known to live there can echolocate.

champ.name: The Bodette-Affolter video
champ.summary: Fisherman Dick Affolter and his stepson Pete Bodette filmed something at the surface that some see as a head and neck with an opening mouth and others as a fish or eel. Two retired FBI image analysts found no tampering, but one said he couldn't actually see an animal in it.

ogopogo.name: MacDougal's horses pulled under
ogopogo.summary: Settler John MacDougal said that while swimming his horses behind his canoe, something dragged them under and nearly took the canoe too, until he cut the line. The story echoes older Syilx accounts of n'ha-a-itk, the spirit of the lake, which travellers left offerings to before crossing.

ogopogo.name: Fifty tourists on a Kelowna beach
ogopogo.summary: About fifty people on a beach said they watched something in the lake for around 45 minutes. Larry Thal, visiting from Vancouver, caught ten seconds of it on 8 mm film. Skeptics suggest a pair of otters.

ogopogo.name: The Chaplin tape
ogopogo.summary: Ken Chaplin and his 78-year-old father staked out log booms with a video camera and filmed a slim animal up to 15 feet long that slapped its tail and dove. Time magazine and Unsolved Mysteries picked it up; local biologists said it was most likely a beaver.

ogopogo.name: The water-skier video
ogopogo.summary: On July 24, 1992, Paul DeMara taped something moving just under the surface as a water skier fell nearby. A forensic video analyst later said it looked like debris from a fallen tree bobbing in the water, and noted the skier didn't react to it at all.

ogopogo.name: Sonar near Rattlesnake Island
ogopogo.summary: A Japanese expedition recorded a 40-foot sonar return about 7 metres down off Rattlesnake Island, the spot long called the creature's home, and found underwater caves. Follow-up trips in 2001 and 2006 were inconclusive.

ogopogo.name: Peachland humps photographed
ogopogo.summary: Photographer Sean Viloria took one picture of two humps off Peachland, then eleven more of a shape near a boat eight days later. MonsterQuest found no tampering; others think it was a windsurfer who had tipped over.

ogopogo.name: Girl Guides see a 45-foot creature in Otter Bay
ogopogo.place: Otter Bay, Okanagan Lake, near Vernon, British Columbia
ogopogo.summary: In July 1928 a patrol of Girl Guides and their nurse, spending a calm, hot day on the shore of Otter Bay, reported a 'long creature' about 45 feet long rushing across the glassy water with an undulating motion that made quite a noise. The wire story teased that the girls needed a new zoology instructor or more shade, but noted that the Ogopogo had been reported before, always in the hottest weather.

thunderbird.name: Tombstone's 'winged monster' on the Huachuca desert
thunderbird.summary: On April 26, 1890, the Tombstone Epitaph ran a story about two ranchers who chased a huge winged creature, like an alligator with an immense pair of wings, across the desert and shot it. Nobody has ever found the photo people later said went with it, and historians treat the piece as a frontier tall tale.
thunderbird.source_title: Lost Media Wiki: the Tombstone Thunderbird photograph

thunderbird.name: 'Body like a naval torpedo' over Alton
thunderbird.summary: In April 1948 several people in Illinois reported an enormous bird. E. M. Coleman and his five-year-old son said they watched it fly over the edge of Alton at about 500 feet, with a body that looked like a naval torpedo. Similar reports came from Caledonia and Belvidere that spring.
thunderbird.source_title: Atlas Obscura: The mythic child-stealing thunderbirds of Illinois

thunderbird.name: Ahead of a storm over Highway 3
thunderbird.summary: A driver heading north on Highway 3 said that in March 2026 he saw a soaring bird that dwarfed the ordinary birds flying in front of it, with a wingspan he guessed at the length of a school bus. He looked away in traffic for a few seconds and it was gone.

jersey-devil.name: Mother Leeds's thirteenth child
jersey-devil.summary: The best-known version of the legend says a Mrs. Leeds, pregnant for the thirteenth time, cursed the baby, which grew wings, hooves and a tail and flew up the chimney into the Pine Barrens. A real Deborah and Japhet Leeds lived at Leeds Point, and Japhet's 1736 will names twelve children.

jersey-devil.name: Ben Franklin's 'ghost' rival
jersey-devil.summary: Historian Brian Regal traces the 'Leeds Devil' to the Leeds family's feuds. Quakers had called almanac maker Daniel Leeds a servant of the devil, and Benjamin Franklin joked for years that his rival Titan Leeds was a ghost. The Leeds family crest even showed a wyvern, a winged, upright dragon.

jersey-devil.name: The engineer who quit his run
jersey-devil.place: Pine Barrens rail line, New Jersey (reprinted in Savannah, Georgia)
jersey-devil.summary: A locomotive engineer told the New York Sun that at dusk one October evening, running through the pines, something with huge silent wings swooped down and thrust its head through the cab window. It had an owl-like head, a sunken white ape-like face, fiery protruding eyes and pointed ears, and it kept pace with the engine at forty miles an hour. His fireman fainted. He struck it between the eyes with the furnace poker and it never flinched. Then it gave another yell and was gone. He said he quit the run soon after.

jersey-devil.name: Hoof prints in pairs at Groveville and Trenton
jersey-devil.place: Groveville, Trenton and Mount Holly, New Jersey
jersey-devil.summary: During the great scare of January 1909, two Trenton-area men reported hoof prints like a small horse's, but set in pairs rather than fours and broken off as if the animal leapt great distances. One set was in a Groveville back yard and one in a city park. At Mount Holly, an elderly resident said a shadow fell across his window at dinner and he looked up to see a huge bird with long, hoofed legs dangling beneath it, flying high overhead.

jersey-devil.name: A 'Jersey devil' found dead near Kinkora
jersey-devil.summary: In October 1909 two young men brought into Burlington the carcass of an animal they had found in the woods near Kinkora, and hundreds came to look. It was about twenty inches long, with a kangaroo-like spine and a squirrel-like tail of reddish fur. Its long, four-jointed forelegs ended in broad, flat, hoof-like bones, which the paper argued could explain the paired prints in the snow the winter before. Something like the frame of short wings rose from its back. The state museum's curator was asked to identify it.

jersey-devil.name: Red wings over Hightown, Virginia
jersey-devil.summary: A Virginia news column reported that a man near Hightown had just seen what neighbours called the famous Jersey devil, flying directly over him. He described a head like a horse's, legs and feet like a mule's, and great red wings. The paper added that something similar had been reported in West Virginia months earlier and was thought to live in the mountains, feeding on bear and deer.

jersey-devil.name: The Leeds devil 'turned up again'
jersey-devil.place: Burlington County, New Jersey (and Mulberry, North Carolina)
jersey-devil.summary: An old Burlington County resident, reading of a strange creature seen in North Carolina with an owl's head, a monkey-like face with white cheeks and an unearthly yell that frightened every dog on the place, declared that it was the Leeds devil. He remembered when it roamed South Jersey fifty years earlier, hunted by men and dogs and shot at by the best marksmen without effect, and retold the century-old legend of its birth.
jersey-devil.source_title: The Morning News (Savannah, Ga.), October 11, 1887, from the New York Sun

owlman.name: Two campers meet an owl 'as big as a man'
owlman.summary: On July 3, 1976, three months after the first report, two 14-year-old girls camping near Mawnan church said they saw a big owl with pointed ears, as big as a man, with glowing eyes and black pincer-like claws. Like the first report, it reached the public through Tony 'Doc' Shiels, who some think made the whole story up.

bessie.name: A dark 40-foot serpent from a schooner
bessie.summary: In July 1817 a schooner's crew reported a dark serpent 30 to 40 feet long. Later that year another crew saw a copper-coloured one about 60 feet long and fired muskets at it, with no effect.

bessie.name: The Dusseau brothers' beached monster
bessie.summary: Two French settler brothers named Dusseau said they found a 20- to 30-foot creature like a sturgeon with arms, thrashing on the beach as if dying. They ran, and when they came back it was gone, leaving marks in the sand and scales the size of silver dollars.

bessie.name: A whole crew sees it wrestling in the water
bessie.place: Lake Erie, between Buffalo and Toledo
bessie.summary: In July 1892 the captain and crew of a ship bound for Toledo said they came on churning water and a 50-foot serpent 'wrestling about as if fighting with an unseen foe', with fins and sparkling eyes, its head four feet out of the water. Local papers carried the story.

bessie.name: Forty-five minutes off Crystal Beach
bessie.place: Crystal Beach, near Fort Erie, Ontario
bessie.summary: On May 5, 1896, four people said they watched a 30-foot creature with a dog-like head and pointed tail churn up the water for 45 minutes before it vanished at dusk.

cadborosaurus.name: A skeleton in the ice at Glacier Island
cadborosaurus.summary: On November 10, 1930, a 24-foot skeleton with flippers was found frozen in ice. Parts went to Cordova to be studied, and it is now thought to have been a whale.

cadborosaurus.name: Henry Island remains
cadborosaurus.place: Henry Island, near Prince Rupert, British Columbia
cadborosaurus.summary: Badly rotted remains about 30 feet long washed up in November 1934. Marine biologist Neal Carter examined them and they were identified as a basking shark, which can rot into a long-necked 'sea serpent' shape.

cadborosaurus.name: 'Sarah the sea hag' on Kitsilano Beach
cadborosaurus.summary: A carcass found on a Vancouver beach was nicknamed Sarah the sea hag before zoologists W. A. Clemens and Ian McTaggart-Cowan identified it as a shark.

cadborosaurus.name: Two police officers and a line of sea lions
cadborosaurus.summary: Inspector Robert Owens and Staff Sergeant Jack Russell saw a huge sea serpent with a horse-like head, until binoculars showed a bull sea lion leading six others. Diving one after another, they looked like a single long body.

cadborosaurus.name: The Kelly Nash video
cadborosaurus.summary: Fisherman Kelly Nash said he filmed ten to fifteen long creatures, young ones among them, in Nushagak Bay. A short clip aired on a Discovery show in 2011; the full tape has never been released.

cadborosaurus.name: The camel-headed serpent gets a name
cadborosaurus.place: Cadboro Point and Chemainus River, Vancouver Island, British Columbia
cadborosaurus.summary: In October 1933 the Associated Press reported that some forty witnesses 'of all degrees,' from fishermen to provincial officials, had now described a camel-headed sea serpent off Vancouver Island, and that Cadboro Point had named it 'Cadborosaurus,' or Caddy. Three Victoria men said they saw it near the Chemainus River, leaving a wake like a speedboat. A man from Oyster River came forward to say that months earlier he had seen an 80-foot animal with six-inch fangs and something like a mane on its head, and had fired two shots at it.

bear-lake-monster.name: Bishop Budge sees a fox-faced swimmer
bear-lake-monster.summary: Latter-day Saint bishop William Budge wrote to the Ogden Junction that he and two friends saw a 5 to 6 foot animal with snuff-coloured fur, a flat face like a huge fox, big blue eyes and ears like a horse's. He said it didn't look fierce and was in no hurry to leave.

bear-lake-monster.name: Brigham Young sends a rope
bear-lake-monster.summary: After Joseph C. Rich's articles in the Deseret News, church leaders visiting Bear Lake Valley said locals considered the sightings indisputable. Brigham Young sent a large rope to Paris, Idaho to help catch the creature, and residents drew up plans for a giant baited hook on a buoy. The Salt Lake Tribune mocked the monster as 'twin brother to the devil and cousin to Brigham'.

flathead-lake-monster.name: Thirteen sightings in one summer
flathead-lake-monster.summary: Flathead Lake usually gets one or two reports a year, but about thirteen came in during 1993. Retired Polson editor Paul Fugleberg, who collected them, said some witnesses were genuinely scared and he shouldn't write about them tongue in cheek.

mokele-mbembe.name: Captain von Stein's report
mokele-mbembe.summary: While surveying the German colony of Cameroon, Captain Ludwig von Stein zu Lausnitz wrote down guides' descriptions of an elephant-sized, smooth-skinned animal with a long flexible neck that overturned canoes and fed on a liana with white flowers. He was shown a path it supposedly made, but there were too many elephant and hippo tracks to tell.

bunyip.name: The word 'bunyip' first appears in print
bunyip.summary: In July 1845 the Geelong Advertiser reported fossil bones that an Aboriginal man identified as a bunyip's. He drew it: a beast with an emu's head and long bill, an alligator's body, and strong claws, standing twelve or thirteen feet tall on its hind legs. It is the first known use of the word in print.

bunyip.name: A 'bunyip or immense platypus' in the Yarra
bunyip.summary: In March 1847 a crowd gathered when something was seen sunning itself on the river opposite Melbourne's Custom House. Three men rowed out to catch it, and it vanished when they were about a yard away.

bunyip.name: The Challicum bunyip outline
bunyip.summary: The Australasian newspaper recorded an outline of a bunyip, about 11 paces long, cut into a creek bank. Local Aboriginal people said it marked a bunyip speared after it killed a man, and they came back each year to re-trace it until the 1850s. The outline no longer exists.

bunyip.name: Stocqueler sketches one on the Murray
bunyip.summary: The artist Stocqueler, paddling down the Murray with his mother to paint river scenes, said he saw a five- or six-foot animal lying on the water, about 25 yards off, before it paddled away. Papers said his drawing looked like a cross between a platypus and a sea serpent. Riverboat captain Francis Cadell couldn't say what it was.

bunyip.name: Four shotgun blasts on a Gundagai lagoon
bunyip.place: Lagoon near Gundagai, New South Wales
bunyip.summary: A Gundagai man told a reporter he and a friend had seen 'a thing that might be a bunyip' on a lagoon near town. It was a little over three feet long and apparently hairy, with a neck like the thick part of a swan's and no clear head, just two ears hanging from the top of the neck. He said it moaned like a bull and spouted water eight feet into the air. He fired four shotgun shots at it, but it went under and never came back up. The wire story ran in American papers under the headline that Loch Ness now had a rival.
bunyip.source_title: Evening Star (Washington, D.C.), October 3, 1947, Sydney wire report

flatwoods-monster.name: Skid marks and a gummy deposit
flatwoods-monster.summary: The sheriff's search on the night of September 12, 1952 found nothing, but the next day A. Lee Stewart Jr. of the Braxton Democrat said he found skid marks in the field and an odd, gummy residue. UFO groups called it a landing site. A meteor had crossed Maryland, Pennsylvania and West Virginia that same evening.

dover-demon.name: John Baxter on Miller Hill Road
dover-demon.summary: A couple of hours after Bill Bartlett's sighting on April 21, 1977, 15-year-old John Baxter said he met a similar small figure on Miller Hill Road. The next night Abby Brabham said she saw it from a car on Springdale Avenue. Plotted on a map, the three spots form a straight line about two miles long.

hopkinsville-goblins.name: Sixteen officers search the farm
hopkinsville-goblins.summary: Worried about a gunfight, four city police, five state troopers, three deputies and four military police from Fort Campbell went to the Sutton farmhouse after the family's report on August 21, 1955. They found broken windows and holes in the screens, likely from the family's own gunfire, and nothing else. The family said the creatures came back at 3:30 a.m.

loveland-frog.name: Three frog-faced figures by the road
loveland-frog.summary: The legend starts with a businessman driving out of Branch Hill late one night who said he saw three upright figures, 3 to 4 feet tall with leathery skin and frog faces, by the road. In some tellings one held up a wand that threw sparks.

loveland-frog.name: The officer who shot an iguana
loveland-frog.summary: Two weeks after Officer Ray Shockey's sighting, Officer Mark Matthews shot a crouching animal in the same spot and found it was a 3-foot iguana missing its tail, probably an escaped pet. He said Shockey agreed it was what he'd seen.

loveland-frog.name: Pokemon Go players see it again
loveland-frog.summary: A couple playing Pokemon Go near the Little Miami River said they saw a frog-like being standing on its hind legs. Asked about it on TV, retired officer Mark Matthews said it was like Bigfoot, and he didn't believe in that either.

lizard-man.name: Airman's shooting story falls apart
lizard-man.summary: On August 5, 1988, Kenneth Orr, an airman from Shaw Air Force Base, said he had shot and wounded the Lizard Man and handed over scales and blood. Two days later he admitted making it up to keep the story going, and was charged with carrying a pistol unlawfully and filing a false report. Radio station WCOS had offered a million dollars for the creature alive.
lizard-man.source_title: Lizard Man of Scape Ore Swamp - Wikipedia

lizard-man.name: A chewed-up van in Bishopville
lizard-man.summary: Twenty years later a Bishopville couple found their vehicle damaged with blood on it, and the Lizard Man was back in the news on CNN. The blood turned out to be from a dog, and the sheriff suggested a coyote or wolf.
lizard-man.source_title: Lizard Man of Scape Ore Swamp - Wikipedia

lizard-man.name: Drinking from Black Creek
lizard-man.place: Lewis Ocean Bay Heritage Preserve, South Carolina
lizard-man.summary: A self-described skeptic said that walking a trail in the preserve he saw a figure crouched by the creek, drinking. When he called out it looked up with a long, lizard-like snout and ran. Where it had been he found three-toed prints heading into the trees.

mongolian-death-worm.name: Locals pick out a sand boa
mongolian-death-worm.summary: Shown a Tartar sand boa, a stout, short-tailed desert snake, local people who said they had seen the olgoi-khorkhoi agreed it was the same animal.

mongolian-death-worm.name: Mackerle's 'thumper'
mongolian-death-worm.summary: Czech explorer Ivan Mackerle led trips in 1990 and 1992 and, inspired by the sandworms of Dune, built a motorised thumper and set off small explosions to draw the worm to the surface. Nothing came up.

mongolian-death-worm.name: A worm lizard, not a killer
mongolian-death-worm.summary: Richard Freeman of the Centre for Fortean Zoology searched and came home empty-handed. He decided the deadly powers were folklore and that witnesses had probably seen an unknown worm lizard.

mongolian-death-worm.name: A TV reporter's interviews
mongolian-death-worm.summary: New Zealand reporter David Farrier joined an August 2009 search and found no worm, but interviewed people who said they had seen one. He noted the sightings peaked in the 1950s.

tatzelwurm.name: Roduner's mountain dragon
tatzelwurm.summary: Andreas Roduner said he met a four-legged, cat-faced 'mountain dragon' that reared up on its hind legs as tall as a man, with bristles like a boar's down its back. Naturalist Johann Jakob Scheuchzer later published it with an engraving.

tatzelwurm.name: The Tinner brothers' cat-headed serpent
tatzelwurm.summary: Among the dragon testimonies Johann Jacob Wagner collected was one from Hans and Thomas Tinner, who said they killed a legless, grey-black serpent with a cat's head, 7 feet or more long. Neighbours had complained that something was sucking their cows' udders, and they said it stopped after that.

honey-island-swamp-monster.name: Four-toed tracks and a dead boar
honey-island-swamp-monster.summary: Harlan Ford and his friend Billy Mills said they found strange footprints and a wild boar with its throat gashed. Casts said to come from the creature show four toes, which no primate has.

honey-island-swamp-monster.name: Film found after Ford's death
honey-island-swamp-monster.summary: When Harlan Ford died, a reel of Super 8 film said to show the creature turned up among his things. Local lore has its own explanation: chimpanzees from a circus train that crashed early in the 20th century.

almas.name: Przhevalsky hears of the 'man-beast'
almas.summary: Explorer Nikolay Przhevalsky wrote down what he was told about the kung-guressu: a flat, human-like face, walking on two legs, thick black fur, huge claws and such strength that people moved their homes away from where it was seen.

almas.name: The Soviet 'snowman commission'
almas.summary: After scientists reported 'snowmen', the USSR sent an expedition to the Pamirs led by hydrologist Alexander Pronin, with historian Boris Porshnev and surgeon Marie-Jeanne Koffman. Porshnev later argued the almas could be surviving Neanderthals; few colleagues agreed.

almas.name: Hair samples tested
almas.summary: Geneticist Bryan Sykes tested eight 'almasty' hair samples from Russia. They came from brown bears, horses and cattle.

yeren.name: Hairy men scale a city wall
yeren.summary: In 650 CE the writer Zhao Yanshou described a band of maoren, 'hairy men', climbing a city wall. Reports of wild men grow more common in Tang dynasty writing.

yeren.name: 'The Minister of Yeren' collects testimony
yeren.summary: Local official Li Jian recorded villagers' yeren sightings going back to 1945, earning himself the nickname the Minister of Yeren. His work drew in university and Academy of Sciences researchers once the Mao era ended.

orang-pendek.name: Van Heerwarden's sedapa in a tree
orang-pendek.summary: Dutch surveyor van Heerwarden described a dark, hairy creature on a branch with hair falling to its waist, long arms and short legs. He said its face was not ugly and not at all ape-like.

kongamato.name: A wounded man and the Prince of Wales
kongamato.summary: Correspondent G. Ward Price wrote that on a tour with the future King Edward VIII they met a man hurt in a feared local swamp. Shown a picture of a pterosaur, he picked it out as his attacker and was badly frightened by it.

kongamato.name: Sanderson and Russell are dive-bombed
kongamato.summary: Naturalists Ivan T. Sanderson and Gerald Russell said a huge black flying creature swooped at them over a river at dusk. Sanderson later suggested it was a giant hammer-headed bat.

kongamato.name: A chest wound and a sketch
kongamato.summary: A man reached hospital with severe chest injuries and said a big bird had attacked him in the Bangweulu Swamps. Asked to draw it, he supposedly sketched something like a pterosaur. Engineer J. P. F. Brown had reported flying reptiles nearby the year before.

kongamato.name: A Telegraph photo turns out to be a stork
kongamato.summary: A photo by Ian Colvin of the Daily Telegraph was claimed to show a pterosaur-like animal. On closer study it was most likely a shoebill or saddle-billed stork.

wendigo.name: The Jesuit Relations describe wendigo sickness
wendigo.summary: Jesuit missionaries reported men seized by a frenzy and craving for human flesh during famine, an early written record of what later writers called wendigo psychosis.

wendigo.name: The Swift Runner case
wendigo.summary: During a starving winter in 1878 to 1879, Cree trapper Swift Runner killed and ate his family, only 25 miles from a Hudson's Bay Company post with food. He said a wendigo spirit had possessed him. He was tried and hanged at Fort Saskatchewan in 1879.

wendigo.name: Jack Fiddler, the wendigo killer, is arrested
wendigo.summary: Oji-Cree chief Jack Fiddler was known for defeating wendigos, which sometimes meant killing people believed to be turning into one. In 1907 Canadian police arrested him and his brother Joseph for murder. Jack took his own life; Joseph was pardoned but died in custody before he heard.

thetis-lake-monster.name: The TV movie that aired days before
thetis-lake-monster.summary: Writer Daniel Loxton found that local TV had shown Monster from the Surf, about a scaly gill-man attacking teenagers on a beach, four days before the Thetis Lake report. The boys' description matched it closely, and one of them later told Loxton they made it up for attention.

indrid-cold.name: The grinning man of Elizabeth
indrid-cold.summary: In his 1970 book Strange Creatures from Time and Space, John Keel wrote that on October 11, 1966 two boys saw a very tall man in shiny green coveralls behind a fence, grinning at them. Keel tied him to Woodrow Derenberger's 'Indrid Cold', and the Grinning Man became part of the Mothman story.

mapinguari.name: A rubber tapper's Sunday story
mapinguari.summary: A rubber tapper quoted in 1928 said he went hunting one Sunday and came back to find the mapinguari eating his workmate in their hut. It had jaguar-like claws and a mouth running from face to stomach. The tale doubles as a warning about working on the Sabbath.

montauk-monster.name: Gawker turns it into a sensation
montauk-monster.summary: After a small item in the local Independent, a photo of the carcass reached Gawker, which ran it on July 29, 2008 as 'Dead Monster Washes Ashore in Montauk'. Theories ran from a shell-less turtle to an escapee from the Plum Island Animal Disease Center. East Hampton's natural resources director said it was a raccoon missing its upper jaw, and most experts agreed.

grootslang.name: Cornell's serpent in the Orange River
grootslang.summary: In The Glamour of Prospecting, gold prospector F. C. Cornell wrote that Khoekhoe people and some settlers along the Orange River feared a huge snake said to live in a rock in the middle of the river and to take cattle from the banks.

barghest.name: The shape-shifter of Darlington
barghest.summary: In the 1870s people near Darlington spoke of a barghest that appeared as a headless man who vanished in flames, a headless lady, a white cat, a rabbit, or a black dog. Like other barghests it was taken as an omen of death.

inkanyamba.name: Tornado stories at Hogsback
inkanyamba.summary: After tornadoes hit the Hogsback area in 1998, many people blamed the inkanyamba, the great serpent of storms. Local potters began making clay inkanyamba figures with horse- or hog-like heads, wings and fish tails.

dingonek.name: Hobley collects more accounts
dingonek.summary: Colonial administrator C. W. Hobley wrote in the journal of the East Africa Natural History Society that he had heard more descriptions of a similar water beast around Lake Victoria, after hunter John Jordan's story was published.

dingonek.name: Maclean's calls it a new species
dingonek.summary: A Maclean's article announced the dingonek as a newly discovered animal. No specimen was ever produced, and Jordan's 1907 story remains the only detailed sighting.

barmanou.name: Magraner's fifty eyewitnesses
barmanou.summary: Spanish zoologist Jordi Magraner began searching the Chitral valleys in 1987 and gathered more than fifty first-hand accounts. Shown his drawings of apes, fossil humans and others, witnesses picked a Neanderthal-like reconstruction. Magraner was murdered in Afghanistan in 2002.

nittaewo.name: Hugh Nevill records the last of the Nittaewo
nittaewo.summary: Explorer Hugh Nevill wrote down a story, passed along four times, that the Veddahs of Leanama had driven the last Nittaewo into a cave in the late 1700s and lit a fire at its mouth. The cave's location was lost when the Leanama Veddahs died out.

waitoreke.name: Von Haast's spotted pelt
waitoreke.summary: Geologist Julius von Haast was said to have got hold of a waitoreke skin: brown with white spots and no webbing between the toes. It sounds more like a quoll, a spotted Australian marsupial that settlers may have tried to introduce, than any otter.

monkey-man-of-delhi.name: Teenage copycats caught
monkey-man-of-delhi.summary: A year after the panic, four teenagers dressed in monkey costumes and robbed vegetable sellers. Police caught them and let them go with a warning. The original scare had produced more than 350 reports, about 60 injuries and two or three deaths from people falling while fleeing.

queensland-tiger.name: A 'striped marsupial cat' in a natural history book
queensland-tiger.summary: A. S. le Souef included a striped marsupial cat in The Wild Animals of Australasia, and the Australian Museum's mammal curator Ellis Troughton repeated it later. Witness reports go back to 1871 and the Aboriginal yarri tradition is older still.

minhocao.name: Saint-Hilaire hears of a lake monster
minhocao.place: Padre Aranda and Feia lakes, Brazil
minhocao.summary: French naturalist Augustin Saint-Hilaire recorded accounts of a minhocao in two lakes that often dragged horses and cattle under. He thought people might be describing a large South American lungfish.

minhocao.name: A dead one with armadillo skin
minhocao.summary: A claim from 1849 described a dead minhocao with skin as thick as pine bark, made of hard scales like an armadillo's. A writer in Nature later wondered if stories like this were a memory of the giant armadillos that once lived in southern Brazil.

lusca.name: A ten-foot octopus on the beach
lusca.summary: J. S. George of Nassau wrote to The American Naturalist about a dead octopus found on the beach, about ten feet long and 200 to 300 pounds, with five-foot arms. It is the first reported find that fits the lusca stories.

lusca.name: The 'giant scuttle' of Hole-in-the-Wall
lusca.summary: The first published description of a Bahamian 'giant scuttle' claimed an arm span of 200 feet, and said tales of 60 to 80 foot spans were common. No octopus is known to come close.

wild-man-of-the-navidad.name: The wild man is captured
wild-man-of-the-navidad.summary: After years of night-time visits, settlers caught a man living in the wild who spoke no English. A sailor who knew his language said he was the son of an African chief, sold into slavery as a child, who had escaped with a companion who later died. He was sold again and died in Victoria, Texas, in 1884, known as Old Jimbo.
wild-man-of-the-navidad.source_title: Wild Man of the Navidad - Wikipedia

wild-man-of-the-navidad.name: A runaway notice for the 'Wild Woman'
wild-man-of-the-navidad.summary: From June to August 1854 the Texas State Gazette ran a runaway slave notice for 'an African well known as the Wild Woman of the Navidad'. The legend's frightening 'wild people' were real people who had escaped slavery.
wild-man-of-the-navidad.source_title: Wild Man of the Navidad - Wikipedia

piasa.name: John Russell invents the Piasa legend
piasa.summary: Writer John Russell published the tale of chief Ouatoga fighting off a man-eating bird, the version most people know today. Folklorists consider it his own invention. The painting Marquette and Jolliet saw in 1673 was a wingless underwater panther; wings were only added in 19th-century drawings.

hobyahs.name: The Hobyahs move to the Australian bush
hobyahs.summary: Victoria's School Paper printed the tale in 1926, and a few years later the Victorian Readers retold it with a 'little dog dingo' in the bush. Generations of Australian children grew up afraid of the Hobyahs as a result.

agogwe.name: Two little brown men among the baboons
agogwe.summary: Cuthbert Burgoyne wrote that from a cargo boat he and his wife watched, through a strong glass, two small upright 'brown men' walk out of the bush onto a beach among feeding baboons, which didn't react. A hunter friend told him of seeing a family of the same creatures nearby.

tylwyth-teg.name: First written mention of the Fair Family
tylwyth-teg.summary: The name Tylwyth Teg first appears in a poem credited to Dafydd ap Gwilym, in which the narrator gets comically lost in fairy mist on his way to see his sweetheart.

leprechaun.name: An 'Irish lubrican' on the London stage
leprechaun.summary: The first known use of the word in English is in Thomas Dekker's play The Honest Whore, Part 2, which mentions 'your Irish lubrican, that spirit'.

gnomes.name: Agricola's mine spirits
gnomes.summary: Mining scholar Georg Agricola wrote down German miners' stories of the Bergmannlein, little mountain men who threw pebbles at miners as a prank but sometimes left them a rich vein of silver. Paracelsus later turned them into his 'gnomes', and the miners' word kobelt for a troublesome ore gave us the name cobalt.

dogman.name: Lumberjacks see a man with a dog's head
dogman.summary: The story usually given as the first Dogman encounter: two lumberjacks said they saw a creature with a man's body and a dog's head. Local lore says it comes back every ten years, in years ending in seven.

dogman.name: Attacked by a pack, one on two legs
dogman.summary: Robert Fortney said five wild dogs attacked him and one of them walked on two legs. Similar creatures were reported in Allegan County in the 1950s and at Cross Village and Manistee in 1967.

dogman.name: Standing behind the car in the driveway
dogman.summary: A man known only as Ben said that in December 1993 he saw an upright canine standing on its hind legs behind a car in his parents' driveway on Lakewood Drive. It ran off when he screamed. In 1994 another driver nearby said he hit something he took for a deer but found only grey fur in the grille.

dogman.name: A cabin break-in at Luther
dogman.summary: After hearing a report of an unknown canine breaking into a cabin near Luther, DJ Steve Cook added new verses to 'The Legend', the April Fool's song that started the Dogman craze. He says he has received more than 100 reports since 1987.

chupacabra.name: Eight sheep with three puncture wounds
chupacabra.summary: In March 1995 eight sheep were found dead with three puncture wounds in the chest, said to be drained of blood. Months later, comedian Silverio Perez coined the name chupacabras on his San Juan radio show, and more than 200 reports followed that year.

chupacabra.name: A hundred animals killed in Calama
chupacabra.summary: In April 2000 about a hundred farm animals in the mining city of Calama were found drained or mutilated, and reports carried on until 2002. One farmer killed a guina, a small wild cat, and the case made international news.

chupacabra.name: The Elmendorf Beast
chupacabra.summary: A rancher shot a hairless dog-like animal attacking his livestock. DNA testing at UC Davis showed it was a coyote with sarcoptic mange, and two more carcasses found nearby that October were the same. Mangy coyotes explain most Texas 'chupacabras'.

chupacabra.name: A deputy's dashcam video
chupacabra.summary: A year after the Cuero carcass, DeWitt County deputy Brandon Riedel filmed a hairless, long-snouted animal with short front legs running down alleys. The sheriff thought it was the same kind of coyote.

chupacabra.name: A roadside carcass in Maine
chupacabra.summary: In August 2006 Michelle O'Donnell photographed a strange dead animal by the road, which her husband said looked like a cross between a rodent and a dog. DNA later showed it was a wolf-dog hybrid.

mothman.name: Connie Carpenter's daylight sighting
mothman.summary: John Keel wrote that on November 27, 1966, Connie Carpenter saw the creature in broad daylight and described glowing red eyes. That same month a hunter shot a snowy owl near Point Pleasant with a wingspan of nearly five feet, which papers called a giant owl.

mothman.name: A photo on Route 2
mothman.summary: WCHS-TV published photos an anonymous driver said showed Mothman on a tree. Science writer Sharon Hill said it looked like a bird, maybe an owl carrying off a frog or snake.

mothman.name: Fifty-five 'Mothman' reports in Chicago
mothman.summary: Researcher Lon Strickler collected 55 reports of a winged humanoid around Chicago in 2017. A University of Chicago psychologist pointed out these were people who chose to come forward to a paranormal website, not a random sample.

gef.name: A slander case over the talking mongoose
gef.summary: BBC Listener editor Richard Lambert, who had investigated Gef with Harry Price, sued Sir Cecil Levita for saying he was unfit to sit on the British Film Institute board because he believed in a talking mongoose. Lambert won substantial damages.

gef.name: The new owner says he shot Gef
gef.summary: After the Irvings sold the farm, new owner Leslie Graham told the press he had shot Gef. The body he showed was black and white and far bigger than the mongoose described, and Voirrey Irving said it wasn't Gef. She maintained to the end of her life that she had not made Gef up.

hodag.name: A 'real hodag' at Lake Minnetonka
hodag.summary: A Minnetonka landowner insisted that a scaly, spined night creature, which he likened to a cross between an iguana and a rocking horse, haunted the woods around his estate. Neighbours said it bellowed like an angry elephant and wallowed in the swamp. He said he had emptied birdshot at it in the moonlight from under thirty yards, heard the pellets rattle off its scales like hail, and hit it twice with a rifle. Each time it ran off with its spiny tail held high, making a sound like a hyena's laugh crossed with a cow's bawl. Hunting parties never caught it.

mystery-airships.name: A phantom airship over Smethport
mystery-airships.summary: In July 1915 a cigar-shaped airship 'not unlike a Zeppelin' was reported hovering over the wild country around Smethport, Pennsylvania, in the small hours for several nights running, flashing green lights. Many townspeople saw it. Campers outside town said its searchlight was repeatedly turned on their tents, and one man heard its motors as it passed about a thousand feet up. With a war on in Europe, some feared German agents meant to attack the explosives plant at Emporium. Search parties set out to find a hidden base in the roadless hills.

wampus-cat.name: The York County varmint
wampus-cat.place: York County, South Carolina, and Mecklenburg and Gaston counties, North Carolina
wampus-cat.summary: For weeks in early 1921 something unseen left tracks across three counties on both sides of the state line and made 'the most mournful, doleful cries.' Scores of hunters and dogs combed the woods in vain. A rural mail carrier fired twice at a large shape he saw in the moonlight taking his chickens. The next morning, at a home nearby, four puppies and two hounds were found dead, their mother fatally bitten after fighting the intruder, with tracks around the place 'as big as a mule's.' Guesses ranged from an escaped coyote or carnival tiger to a panther. The headline called it a wampus.
wampus-cat.source_title: The Abbeville Press and Banner (Abbeville, S.C.), March 4, 1921

wampus-cat.name: A 'willapus-wampus' near Emory University
wampus-cat.place: Clairmont Avenue near Emory University, Atlanta, Georgia
wampus-cat.summary: In May 1923 a mysterious night animal was reported killing dogs, pigs and calves around a floral company's farm near Emory University. Witnesses said it slipped ghost-like through the dark, slashed its victims' throats and seemed to drain their blood. Searchers lay in wait for nights without catching it and found enormous footprints unlike any local animal's. A former mayor of Charleston, Georgia, said it reminded him of the 'willapus-wampus' that had terrorized his countryside about a dozen years earlier.

loch-ness-monster.name: Nessie back after the war
loch-ness-monster.summary: In April 1947, after wartime claims that Nessie had been killed by a bomb, the Inverness-shire county clerk said he had just watched the monster cross the loch diagonally at high speed and submerge about 200 yards from shore. Four men in a car also reported it, disagreeing over whether it had one hump or two. A naval captain who supported the sightings said so many people had now reported it that their accounts could not be put down to romancing, poor eyesight or hysteria.

sea-serpent.name: Becalmed beside it off Stonington
sea-serpent.summary: Captain Powers of the ship Albatross wrote that his vessel lay becalmed about five miles off Stonington when a man aloft spotted something off the lee bow. The captain climbed to the maintop with a good sea glass and watched the animal lie almost motionless at the surface for about fifteen minutes before it slowly turned across the ship's bows. The sea was unusually smooth and clear, every hand on board came to look, and he judged it at no less than twenty feet, with a large oval head and a square, blunt upper jaw. The Tribune printed his statement while openly doubting it.
sea-serpent.source_title: New-York Daily Tribune, September 15, 1845, from the Woonsocket Patriot

sea-serpent.name: Fishermen fire on a Cumberland River monster
sea-serpent.summary: A farmer living about a mile below the city had been losing pigs for months without explanation. Then a party of fishermen taking in a trotline near a small island saw what they took for a swimming animal's head, rowed closer, and watched a scaly creature rise six feet out of the water, with ear-like flaps and a serpent's head and body. One man fired several revolver shots at it. Thirty or forty feet away a sharp tail broke the surface and thrashed the water, and the party pulled away fast. The paper said it told the story just as it was told to them.

sea-serpent.name: A Quaker who ran along Lynn Beach after it
sea-serpent.summary: A correspondent walked the beach with an elderly member of the Society of Friends who, years before, had been one of a small group to see the famous Massachusetts sea serpent. Hearing it had been sighted, he went down to the beach doubting the report, then followed the thing along the shore at a run for twenty minutes. It looked like a huge eel, he said, well over a hundred feet long, sometimes lifting an eel-like head. He insisted he knew how porpoises move at every speed and was not excited in the least.

sea-serpent.name: Moonlight picnickers on the Des Moines River
sea-serpent.place: Des Moines River bridge north of Boone, Iowa
sea-serpent.summary: A group of young people from Boone took the interurban car out to the river bridge on a bright moonlit evening. While they were singing, one of them told the others to look at the water, where a long black animal was playing near the shore, its back showing above the surface in several small arches. They first thought it was a drifting log until it turned and splashed. When some of the men went down the bank for a closer look, it darted off downriver. They almost kept quiet about it, and the paper noted a similar creature had been reported near Humboldt.

ufo-orbs.name: What the bomber crews called foo fighters
ufo-orbs.place: Over Germany and the Rhine Valley (reported in Washington, D.C.)
ufo-orbs.summary: As flying saucer reports swept the country in July 1947, the Evening Star reminded readers what American aircrews had seen over Germany in the winter of 1944 to 1945. Some glowing objects gave off a reddish light and others looked like silver globes. They danced off wingtips, played tag with fighters in power dives, flew in formation, or trailed bombers while flashing on and off. One reportedly chased a pilot twenty miles down the Rhine Valley at 300 miles an hour. Intelligence first feared a radar-jamming weapon, and nobody ever explained them.
